documentation:
ASCII art drawings are rendered as SVG images. This variant uses a fence of many backticks. The shorter form is a code block with the language ascii (see lia-ascii). The fence must not be indented.

Examples:

  `````````````````````````````````
                           .--->  F
  A       B     C   D     /
  *-------*-----*---*----*----->  E
           \            ^ \
            v          /   '--->  G
             B --> C -'
  `````````````````````````````````
label: lia-ascii-example

documentation:
Style an ASCII art drawing with an HTML comment directly above it, e.g. to center it, limit its width or change the colors of lines (stroke) and filled shapes (fill).

Examples:

  <!-- style="display: block;
              margin-left: auto;
              margin-right: auto;
              max-width: 315px;" -->
  ``` ascii
                           .--->  F
      A       B     C   D     /
      *-------*-----*---*----*----->  E
               \            ^ \
                v          /   '--->  G
                 B --> C -'
  ```
label: lia-ascii-example-css

documentation:
A code block with the language ascii is rendered as an SVG image (svgbob). The fence must start at the left margin, an indented block is shown as plain code.

Drawing vocabulary:
  - _ |  \ /       lines
  +                 square corner
  . , ' `           rounded corners
  * # o O           dots, also as arrow ends
  < > ^ v V A       arrow heads
  Unicode box-drawing characters and emojis are also allowed.

Example:
  ``` ascii
  +------+   +-----+
  | Foo  +-->| Bar |
  +------+   +--+--+
                |
                v
          .-----------.
          |  rounded  |
          '-----------'
  ```
label: lia-ascii

documentation:
Text after the language ascii (on the same line as the opening fence) is shown as a caption below the image. It can contain Markdown.

Example:
  ``` ascii  Fig.: A __simple__ box
  +-----+
  | Box |
  +-----+
  ```
insertText:
``` ascii  Fig.: Working with branches in git
new feature      .---#---.
                 |       |
development    .-o---o---o----o----o-.
main   *---*-+-*---*---*-------------*----
```
label: lia-ascii-title

documentation:
Text in double quotes inside an ASCII drawing is not drawn, but rendered as LiaScript on top of the image: Markdown, formulas, animations, quizzes, ... Lines whose quotes start at the same column form one multi-line block. The placement is not pixel-precise, so adjust the quotes and the frame by hand.

Example:
  ``` ascii
  +-------------------------------------------+
  | "$ \sum_{i=1}^n i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} $"   |
  +-------------------------------------------+
  | "Gauss found this at the age of __9__."   |
  +-------------------------------------------+
  ```
label: lia-ascii-embed

documentation: Inline `code` has `back-ticks around` it.
label: lia-code-inline

documentation: To insert a code block with syntax highlight, enclose your code snippet with three back-ticks (```) that is followed by a language code. To search all language codes, visit the link below, but in most cases you can simply add either the name of the language or the typical file-ending. Examples: ```javascript var s = "JavaScript syntax highlighting"; alert(s); s; ``` ```python s = "Python syntax highlighting" print(s) ``` ``` No language indicated, so no syntax highlighting. But let's throw in a tag. ```
label: lia-code-block

documentation:
To insert an executable and editable code block with syntax highlight, insert a common Markdown code block with a succeeding <script> tag. The macro @input is replaced with the current user input and gets evaluated in a try and catch block. Using JavaScript you can also insert interpreters to other languages or access them. In these cases you will have to change the content of the script tag. To get an impression about the possibilities, click on the link below.
The result of the script or the error are passed to a command-line like output beneath the code-block.

Example:

  ```javascript
  var s = "JavaScript syntax highlighting";
  alert(s);
  ```
  <script>@input</script>
label: lia-code-block-js

documentation:
You can name your snippets by adding just after the language code. At default, it will be visible, but by adding a plus (+) in front of your filename you can make this more expressible, whereby a minus (-) will hide it at first. In this way you can also group multiple files into a (executable) project.

Examples:

  ```javascript    Visible.js
  alert("Visible JavaScript file");
  ```

  ```javascript   +Visible.js
  alert("Also visible JavaScript file");
  ```

  ```javascript   -Hidden.js
  alert("Hidden JavaScript file on init");
  ```
label: lia-code-block-name

documentation:
To insert a named and executable and code snippet. The macro @input is replaced with the current user input and gets evaluated in a try and catch block. Using JavaScript you can also insert interpreters to other languages or access them. In these cases you will have to change the content of the <script> tag. To get an impression about the possibilities, click on the link below.
The result of the script or the error are passed to a command-line like output beneath the code-block.

Example:

  ```javascript   +Visible.js
  var s = "Visible JavaScript syntax highlighting";
  ```
  <script>@input</script>

  ```javascript   -Hidden.js
  var s = "Hidden JavaScript syntax highlighting";
  ```
  <script>@input</script>
label: lia-code-block-name-js
lia-code-block-jsx

insertText:
<script>
  try{
    eval(`@input`);
  } catch (e) {
    var log = e.stack.match(/((.*?):(.*))\n.*?(:(\d+):(\d+)\)\n)/);
    var err_msg = new LiaError(log[1] + " =>  (" + log[4], 1);
    err_msg.add_detail(0, log[3], "error", log[5]-1, log[6]);
    throw err_msg;
  }
</script>
label: lia-code-js

documentation:
Default output: a code block with @output after the language is not shown as code, its content is shown in the terminal of an executable project when the slide loads. It is replaced by the real result after the first execution. This is useful for courses that are read offline or on GitHub, where nothing can be executed. The @output block has to be the last block of the project. A plus (+) shows the content as normal output (stdout), a minus (-) as an error (stderr).

Example:

  ``` js     -EvalScript.js
  let str = "hello world";

  consolelog(str)
  ```
  ``` text    -@output
  There is an error in line 3 ...
  ```
  <script>@input</script>
label: lia-code-output
lia-code-project

documentation: Executable code with asynchronous results. End the script with "LIA: wait", so that LiaScript keeps the code block in the running state. Send output later with send.lia(...) or console.log(...) and finish with send.lia("LIA: stop"). Useful control strings and functions: "LIA: wait" keep running (async) "LIA: stop" finish the execution "LIA: clear" clear the terminal send.lia("text") print output and keep running send.lia("text", [], true) print as success send.lia("text", [], false) print as error send.liascript("## md") render LiaScript in the output send.lia("HTML: x") render raw HTML in the output console.log/warn/error/debug(...) Example: ```js let i = 0 const id = setInterval(() => console.log(i++), 500) setTimeout(() => { clearInterval(id); send.lia("LIA: stop") }, 3000) ```
insertText:
```js
// asynchronous code
setTimeout(() => console.log("done"), 1000)
```
<script>
  eval(`@input`)
  setTimeout(() => send.lia("LIA: stop"), 2000)
  "LIA: wait"
</script>
label: lia-code-async

documentation:
An interactive terminal (REPL): ending the script with "LIA: terminal" opens an input line below the output after execution. send.handle("input", callback) is called for every line the user sends, send.handle("stop", callback) when the user stops the execution.

Example:
  ```js
  // execute me and type 2+2 into the terminal
  ```
  <script>
    send.handle("input", (input) => send.lia(String(eval(input))))
    "LIA: terminal"
  </script>
label: lia-code-terminal

documentation:
Code blocks (executable or not) are rendered with the Ace editor. An HTML comment directly above the block configures it:

  data-showGutter="false"         hide the line numbers
  data-theme="monokai"            any Ace theme
  data-marker="y1 x1 y2 x2 color type;"
                                  highlight a range, repeatable with ;
                                  color: error, log, warn, debug, info
                                         or rgba(...) without spaces
                                  type:  fullLine (default), text,
                                         screenLine
  data-tabSize, data-fontSize, data-firstLineNumber

Example:
  <!-- data-theme="chaos" data-marker="1 0 1 12 warn;" -->
  ```js
  let a = 1
  a = a + 1
  ```
insertText:
<!-- data-showGutter="false" data-theme="chaos" data-marker="1 0 2 20 error text;" -->
```js
let a = 1
let b = a +
```
label: lia-code-style

documentation:
A multi-file project with a default output. Blocks written directly one after another (no blank line) form a project with one shared script. @input(n) refers to the n-th block (counting from 0). A file name with - starts minimized, with + (default) visible. The last block marked with @output is shown in the terminal before the first execution.

Example:
  ``` js     -EvalScript.js
  let who = data.first_name + " " + data.last_name;
  data.online ? who + " is online" : who + " is NOT online"
  ```
  ``` json   +Data.json
  { "first_name": "Sammy", "last_name": "Shark", "online": true }
  ```
  ``` text   +@output
  Is Sammy Shark really online?
  ```
  <script>
    let data = @input(1);
    @input(0)
  </script>

documentation:
Narration comments: the paragraph below --{{n}}-- is read out loud by the text-to-speech engine when animation step n is reached. Only one paragraph is allowed per comment, Markdown can be used inside.

In Presentation mode the text is spoken and hidden, in Slides mode it is spoken and shown in a side panel, and in Textbook mode it is shown in place. A comment never reveals anything on the slide by itself, so pair it with a {{n}} block for the same step (see lia-effect-presentation). Several comments with the same number are read one after another.
The default voice is defined within the main header, if not english will be used. This main voice can be changed per section by adding a section comment.

Example:
  <!--
  author:   ...
  email:    ...
  ...
  narrator: UK English Female
  -->

  # Title

               --{{0}}--
  I will speak with a female *UK* accent.

  ## Section
  <!-- narrator: US English Male -->

               --{{0}}--
  This entire section will be spoken by an American man.

               --{{1}}--
  But only this section...

To simplify the voice-search, simply start typing "voice" and fuzzy search all responsive voice or click on the link below.
insertText:
--{{number}}--
Enter some **text** that gets read out aloud.
Only paragraphs are allowed!
label: lia-comment

documentation:
You can change the voice also per comment by adding it directly after the number of appearance.
Type "voice" for fuzzy searching all responsive voices or click on the link below.

Example:
        --{{0 Australian Female}}--
  I will speak with a female Australian accent,
  no matter what the default language is.

        --{{0 Deutsch Male}}--
  Und hier äußert sich gerade ein deutscher Mann.
insertText:
--{{number voice}}--
Enter some **text** that gets read out aloud with another voice.
Only paragraphs are allowed!
label: lia-comment-voice

documentation:
If you want to speak out some additional text that shall not appear in the textbook mode, then simply put your comment into a HTML comment tag.

Example:
  <!-- --{{2}}--
  I will speak with the default voice, but not appear
  elsewhere within the document.
  -->
insertText: <!-- --{{number}}-- Enter some **text** that gets read out aloud! -->
label: lia-comment-hidden

documentation:
If you want to speak out some additional text that shall not appear in the textbook mode and speak with another voice, then simply put your comment with a voice definition into a HTML comment tag.

Example:
  <!-- --{{2 Deutsch Female}}--
  I will speak with a German voice, but not appear
  elsewhere within the document.
  -->

Type "voice" for fuzzy searching or click on the link below for more information.
insertText: <!-- --{{number voice}}-- Enter some **text** that gets read out aloud! -->
label: lia-comment-voice-hidden

documentation:
Multimedia comment: attach an audio (or video) link at the end of a narration comment to play your own recording at this animation step instead of the text-to-speech voice. The file is only loaded and played when the step is reached in Presentation or Slides mode. It never shows up as a visible player. For a visible player, put the audio link outside of a comment.

Example:
      --{{1}}--
  To play an audio file during your animation step,
  simply attach the link at the end of your comment.
  ?[⏯](recording/audio_1.mp3)
insertText:
--{{number}}--
This text is not spoken, the recording is played instead.
?[⏯](audio.mp3)
label: lia-comment-media

The character is used as a color code, such as r stands for red, w for white, etc. Uppercase and lowercase characters define the size of the plotted dots. And if there is only one character, then it is plotted as a single dot only.

Example:

     6 | A a B b C c
       | D d E e F f G g H h I i
y-axis | J j K k L l M m N n o O
       | P p Q q R r S s T t U u
       | V v W w X x Y y Z Z   *
     1 +------------------------
       0        x-axis        24

The definition of the title, x and y labels and their limits is optional, but the number of used pipes (|) and hyphens (-) define the resolution of the diagram.

The character is used as a color code, such as r stands for red, B for blue, etc. Uppercase and lowercase characters define the size of the plotted dots. A sequence of equal characters gets interpreted as a poly-line, there are more than two characters and if there are no two characters at the same x position.

Example:

    y |               *     *
    - | r r r r r r r*r r r r*r r r r r r r
    a |             *         *
    x |            *           *
    i | B B B B B * B B B B B B * B B B B B
    s |         *                 *
      | *  * *                       * *  *
   -1 +------------------------------------
      0            x-axis                 1

The definition of the title, x and y labels and their limits is optional, but the number of used pipes (|) and hyphens (-) define the resolution of the diagram.

Use simple inline effects to highlight specific elements within a Markdown block. Simply enclose your elements within two subsequent braces ({}{}), whereby the first one is used to hold the number of appearance, while the will contain your text, image, video, what so ever ...
You can tweak your effects with additional animations and styling. Animate.css is included at default.

Examples:
  This block contains some {1}{inline __effects__} that will appear {2}{subsequently}.

  Inline effects can also contain more effects {1}{I will appear first {2}{and I as a second}}.

  With styling ++ {3}{bouncing red and delayed}<!--
        class = "animated infinite bounce"
        style = "animation-delay: 3s; color: red;"
      -->
label: lia-effect-inline

documentation:
Use simple inline effects to highlight specific elements within a Markdown block. Simply enclose your elements within two subsequent braces ({}{}), whereby the first one contains two numbers separated by (-) the first number defines the time of appearance and the second one the time of disappearance. The element contains the Markdown elements for highlighting (text, videos, images, etc.)
You can tweak your effects with additional animations and styling. Animate.css is included at default.

Examples:
  This block contains some {1-2}{I appear at fragment 1 and disapper at 2}.

  Nesting is allowed but has to make sense {1-3}{I will rest from 1 to 3 {4}{I will not be visible}}.

  With styling ++ {1-3}{bouncing red and delayed}<!--
        class = "animated infinite bounce"
        style = "animation-delay: 3s; color: red;"
      -->
label: lia-effect-inline2

documentation:
Use block effects to let an entire Markdown block appear at a certain animation step. Put the step number in double braces on its own line directly above the block. Indent it by 4 or more spaces, so that other Markdown viewers show it as code and not as text. In Textbook mode all blocks are visible and tagged with their step number.
The entire block can also be styled and the animation tweaked, but the required comment tag has to be defined before the Markdown block. Animate.css is included at default.

Examples:
                    {{1}}
  This entire block will appear with the first
  fragment. And remain till the end of this slide.

                    {{2}}
  ```js
  // this works with any markdown block
  ```

  <!-- class = "animated rollIn" -->
       {{3}}
  | Also | with  |
  |------|-------|
  | any  | table |
label: lia-effect-block
lia-effect-block2

Examples:

  Both blocks will appear at once. Nesting of other
  {2}{inline} and block effects is also allowed.

With this triangle notation it is possible to add a playback button, which will read out loud the text within the second braces. It is possible to add additional animation definitions and also to change the voice.

Start typing voice, if you want to change the narrator and the language.

Examples:

Adds a play button to the block below, which reads it out loud with the given voice instead of the default narrator. The button works in every mode and does not depend on the animation steps.

Type "voice" to search all available voices.

Example:

  This paragraph is read with an Australian voice.

Groups multiple blocks into one animation step with an HTML section tag instead of two lines of asterisks. Leave a blank line after <section> and before </section>, so that the content is parsed as Markdown.

Example:
                    {{1}}
  <section>

  This paragraph and the table below appear together.

  | Also | with  |

  | any  | table |

  </section>

{{number}}
<section>

Insert your Markdown blocks in here ...

documentation:
A slide that works as a presentation and as a textbook: every visible step {{n}} is paired with a narration --{{n}}-- for the same step. Think of {{n}} as the bullet point and --{{n}}-- as the speaker notes for it.

How the narration is shown depends on the mode:
  Presentation -> spoken, text hidden
  Slides       -> spoken, text shown in the side panel
  Textbook     -> not spoken, text shown in place

A --{{n}}-- comment alone never reveals anything on the slide, so always pair it with a {{n}} block. Step 0 introduces the slide.

Example:
  ## Photosynthesis

               --{{0}}--
  Plants turn light into sugar. Let us look at the inputs.

                 {{1}}
  * Light, water and CO2 go in

               --{{1}}--
  Three things are needed: light, water and carbon dioxide.
insertText:
## Slide Title

             --{{0}}--
Introduction, spoken when the slide is opened.

               {{1}}
* First bullet point

             --{{1}}--
Narration for the first bullet point.

               {{2}}
* Second bullet point

             --{{2}}--
Narration for the second bullet point.
label: lia-effect-presentation

documentation:
Links can be added in many ways to a document (relative or absolute), either in common Markdown style by enclosed brackets ([]) and parentheses (()), or directly if it starts with http or www and matches the common url pattern.
If you want to navigate within the current document, use hash tag and the number of the slide.
And you can add additional html and css options by adding a trailing comment.

Examples:
  [LiaScript](https://liascript.github.io)

  Also an accepted link: https://liascript.github.io

  Local navigation by slide number: [top](#1)

  Local navigation by slide title: [top](#some-title)

  Autolink, no escaping of parentheses needed: <https://example.com/path_(with_parens)>

  With styling [LiaScript](https://liascript.github.io)<!--
    title = "click me"
    style = "color: red;"
  -->
label: lia-link

documentation:
An optional information can be attached to every link by adding double quotes after the link in the parentheses.

Examples:
  [LiaScript](https://liascript.github.io "click Me")

  Local navigation:
    [top](#1 "by slide number")
    [top](#and-the-title-is "by slide title")
label: lia-link-info

documentation:
Include images via the common Markdown notation as depicted below, by using absolute or relative paths. In contrast to common Markdown you can add also styles, classes, or any other allowed image tag to it simply by appending a comment tag.

Example:

  ![image of a puppy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Puppy_on_Halong_Bay.jpg)

  ![relative](./img/puppy.jpg)

  ![with styling](./img/puppy.jpg)<!--
      title = "a gray puppy"
      width = "300px"
      style = "border: 10px solid; filter: grayscale(100%);"
    -->
label: lia-image

documentation:
Optional information can be attached to every image by adding double quotes after the link in the parentheses. This will be attached as a subtitle to this element and can also include Markdown syntax.

Example:

  ![image of a puppy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Puppy_on_Halong_Bay.jpg "This image is free __CC0__")

  ![relative](./img/puppy.jpg "A cute image of a __puppy__")
label: lia-image-info

documentation:
Including audio is done with a starting question mark (?) that is followed a common Markdown link. If you want to include soundcloud, then you only have to refer to the link and the player gets embedded into your course.

Example:

  ?[singing birds](https://bigsoundbank.com/UPLOAD/mp3/1068.mp3)

  ?[soundcloud](https://soundcloud.com/glennmorrison/beethoven-moonlight-sonata)
label: lia-audio

documentation:
An optional information can be attached to every audio file by adding double quotes after the link in the parentheses. This will be attached as a subtitle to this element and can also include Markdown syntax.

Example:

  ?[singing birds](https://bigsoundbank.com/UPLOAD/mp3/1068.mp3 "optional infos")
label: lia-audio-info

documentation:
Include movies is like combining images and sound by a starting exclamation mark followed by a question mark (!?) as depicted below. Paths can either be absolute or relative. You can add also styles, classes, or any other allowed options to it simply by appending a comment tag.

To simplify the usage, you can directly use the YouTube link, or Vimeo, or TeacherTube. Those resources are atomatically parsed and included appropriately into the document, without searching for an embed-code.

Example:

  !?[eLab](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bICfKRyKTwE)

  !?[relative](./mov/video.mp4)

  !?[eLab](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bICfKRyKTwE)<!--
      title = "the elab in gray"
      width = "90%"
      style = "border: 10px solid; filter: grayscale(100%);"
    -->

But it is still possible to use HTML to include Videos and other stuff ...

  <iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/bICfKRyKTwE" frameborder="0" allow="autoplay; encrypted-media" allowfullscreen></iframe>
label: lia-movie

documentation:
Optional information can be attached to every video by adding double quotes after the link in the parentheses. This will be attached as a subtitle to this element and can also include Markdown syntax.

Example:

  !?[eLab](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bICfKRyKTwE "Some information about the previous __eLab__ project.")
label: lia-movie-info

documentation:

Example:

  ??[Pottery Jar 3D model](https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/pottery-jar-0576d43d28924c948ed3bbae02e4e0cb)

documentation:
If you group multimedia links within one line or within one block, they will appear as a gallery within LiaScript.

Example:

  ![image of a puppy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c7/Puppy_on_Halong_Bay.jpg)
  ??[circuit simulator](https://falstad.com/circuit/circuitjs.html)

documentation:
A link with the text qr-code is rendered as a QR code for its URL, e.g. so that students in a lecture can open a link on their phones. Other Markdown viewers show a normal link.

Example:
  [qr-code](https://liascript.github.io)
label: lia-qr-code

documentation:
A link with the text preview-lia to the raw URL of another LiaScript course is rendered as a preview card with the title, description, logo and author taken from the course header. Clicking the card opens the course.

Example:
  [preview-lia](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/liaScript/docs/master/README.md)
label: lia-preview-lia

documentation:
Links with mailto: open the email program, links with tel: start a phone call on mobile devices.

Example:
  [Write me](mailto:you@example.com)

  [Call me](tel:+491234567890)
label: lia-mailto

documentation:
Two-column layout: an image followed directly by text (no blank line between them) forms one paragraph. The image floats to the left with up to 50% of the width and the text flows beside it. A blank line between image and text puts the text below the image instead.

Example:
  ![A lion](img/lion.jpg "The king of the jungle")
  Lions live in groups called prides. This text is shown
  to the right of the image.
insertText:
![alt-text](image-url "caption")
This text has no blank line before it, so it stays in the same
paragraph as the image and flows beside it.
label: lia-image-float

documentation:
Inline Footnotes are composed of a reference in brackets with a starting caret. The following text has to be put into parentheses, only one line is allowed.

   Example with [^1](inline _footnote_) and some more text.
label: lia-footnote-inline

documentation:
Multiline footnotes have to be split into a reference and into a comment. Footnote references are defined by brackets with a starting caret and can appear everywhere within the text. Footnote texts have to be put at the end of the same section, because LiaScript parses every slide on its own. The id can be a number, a word or even an emoji.

Example:

Here is a footnote reference, [^1] and another.[^longnote]

...

[^1]: Here is the footnote text.

[^longnote]: Here's one with multiple blocks.

               Subsequent paragraphs are indented to show that they
               belong to the previous footnote.
label: lia-footnote-reference

documentation:
Multiline footnotes have to be split into a reference and into a comment. Footnote texts start with a reference "tag", which is followed by a colon. They have to be put into the end of each section otherwise they are not interpreted as footnote texts and multi-block footnotes have to follow the previous indentation.
Example:
...

[^1]: Here is the footnote text.

[^longnote]: Here's one with multiple blocks.

               Subsequent paragraphs are indented to show that they
               belong to the previous footnote.
label: lia-footnote-text

documentation:
Insert a mathematical formula (inline) within your text. It has to be enclosed with two single dollar signs, as shown in the example.

Example: $ f(a,b,c) = (a^2+b^2+c^2)^3 $

Formulas are rendered with KaTeX. Only LaTeX is allowed between the dollar signs, no Markdown or HTML. Click on the link below for all supported commands.
label: lia-formula-inline

documentation:
Insert a more multiline mathematical formula as a block, which is automatically centered within your document. It has to be enclosed with two dollar signs, as shown in the example.

Example:

$$
   \sum_{i=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^2}
        =\frac{\pi^2}{6}
$$

Formulas are rendered with KaTeX. Only LaTeX is allowed between the dollar signs, no Markdown or HTML. Click on the link below for all supported commands.
label: lia-formula-block

documentation:
Chemical equations with the mhchem extension of KaTeX: write the formula inside \ce{...}. Arrows, charges, states and isotopes are supported.

Example:
  $\ce{CO2 + C -> 2 CO}$

  $\ce{Hg^2+ ->[I-] HgI2 ->[I-] [Hg^{II}I4]^2-}$
label: lia-formula-chem

documentation:
Define your own KaTeX macros in the main header (or a section header) with formula:. They can be used in every formula of the course. The line can be repeated for more macros.

Example:
  <!--
  formula: \R      \mathbb{R}
  formula: \norm   \left\lVert #1 \right\rVert
  -->

  # Main

  $ x \in \R $ and $ \norm{x} $
label: lia-formula-macro

documentation:
The main header is an HTML comment at the very top of the document. It defines the defaults of the course: authors, contact, version, language, the narrator voice, additional JavaScript and CSS, macros and more. Continuation lines have to be indented. Most settings can be overwritten per section (see lia-header-section).

Common fields:
  author      separate multiple authors with ;
  email       contact shown in the info panel
  version     0.x.x = development, nothing is stored;
              >= 1.0.0 = quiz, code and task states are stored
              (bump the major version when you move quizzes)
  language    UI language and typography (en, de, fr, es, ...)
  narrator    default text-to-speech voice (type "voice")
  comment     short description for the course card
  logo        image for the course card
  icon        replaces the default LiaScript icon
  mode        Presentation | Slides | Textbook
  repository  link to the source repository
  edit        true or a URL to edit the course online
  link        additional CSS files, one per line
  script      additional JavaScript files, one per line
  import      macros of other courses/templates
  translation link to a translated version

Type "lia-macro-" to find snippets for single header fields.

Example:
  <!--
  author:   Your Name
  email:    your@email.com
  version:  0.1.0
  language: en
  narrator: US English Female

  comment:  A short description of your course.
            Multiline is also okay.

  logo:     ./img/logo.png

  link:     https://cdn.example.com/library.css
  script:   https://cdn.example.com/library.js

  translation: Deutsch  translations/German.md
  -->

  # Course Title

The values can be referred to by the macros @author, @email, @version and @date.
insertText:
<!--
author:   Your Name
email:    your@email.com
version:  0.1.0
language: en
narrator: US English Female

comment:  A short description of your course.
          Multiline is also okay.

logo:     ./img/logo.png
-->
label: lia-header-main

documentation:
A section header is an HTML comment directly after a heading. It overwrites settings of the main header for this section only, e.g. the author, the narrator voice, macros, additional scripts or styles (link, script), formula macros or persistent.

Example:
  # Course

  ## Section
  <!--
  narrator: Australian Female
  -->

  This section is read with an Australian voice.

  ### Sub Section
  <!--
  author:     Section Author
  email:      section.author@email.com
  persistent: true
  -->
insertText:
<!--
author:   Section Author
narrator: UK English Female
-->
label: lia-header-section

documentation:
Initialize your file with a complete example course (header and body), which can be used as a starting point. It shows the most important features: narration and animations, media, ASCII art, charts, quizzes, surveys and executable code.

Example:

    <!--
    author:   Your Name
    email:    your@mail.org
    version:  0.0.1
    language: en
    narrator: US English Female
    ...
    -->

    # Course Main Title

    This is your course initialization stub...
insertText:
<!--
author:   Your Name

email:    your@mail.org

version:  0.0.1

language: en

narrator: US English Female

comment:  Try to write a short comment about
          your course, multiline is also okay.
-->

# Course Main Title

This is your **course** initialization stub.

Please see the [Docs](https://liascript.github.io/course/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/liaScript/docs/master/README.md)
to find out what is possible in [LiaScript](https://liascript.github.io).

> [!TIP]
> Type **lia** in your editor to see all available snippets,
> **voice** for all narrator voices and **hili** for syntax highlighting.

> [!NOTE]
> A version 0.x.x marks a course in development, nothing is stored.
> Switch to 1.0.0 when you publish the course, then the states of
> quizzes, tasks and code are stored in the browser.

## Markdown

You can use common [Markdown](https://github.com/adam-p/markdown-here/wiki/Markdown-Cheatsheet) syntax to create your course, such as:

1. Lists
2. ordered or

   * unordered
   * ones ...


| Header 1   | Header 2   |
| :--------- | :--------- |
| Item 1     | Item 2     |


Images:

![images](https://farm2.static.flickr.com/1618/26701766821_7bea494826.jpg)


## Presentation

             --{{0}}--
This text is spoken when the slide is opened. In Textbook mode it is
shown as normal text.

     {{1}}
* The first point appears at step 1.

             --{{1}}--
And this text explains the first point.

     {{2}}
* The second point appears at step 2.

             --{{2}}--
Insert any kind of audio file:

     {{3}}
?[audio](https://bigsoundbank.com/UPLOAD/mp3/1068.mp3)

     {{4}}
!?[video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bICfKRyKTwE)


### Styling

<!-- class = "animated rollIn" style = "animation-delay: 2s; color: purple" -->
The whole text-block should appear in purple color and with a wobbling effect.
Which is a **bad** example, please use it with caution ...
~~ only this is red ;-) ~~ <!-- class = "animated infinite bounce" style = "color: red;" -->

## Diagrams

``` ascii  Fig.: ASCII art is rendered as an image
+------+   +-----+   +-----+
|      |   |     |   |     |
| Foo  +-->| Bar +-->| Baz |
|      |   |     |   |     |
+------+   +-----+   +-----+
```

Tables with numbers can be shown as charts:

<!-- data-show data-title="Powers" data-xlabel="x" data-ylabel="y" -->
| x | square | cube |
| - | -----: | ---: |
| 0 |      0 |    0 |
| 1 |      1 |    1 |
| 2 |      4 |    8 |
| 3 |      9 |   27 |

## Quizzes

### A Textquiz

What did the **fish** say when he hit a **concrete wall**?

    [[dam]]
    [[?]] It is a pun.

### Multiple Choice

Just add as many points as you wish:

    [[X]] Only the **X** marks the correct point.
    [[ ]] Empty ones are wrong.
    [[X]] ...

### Single Choice

Just add as many points as you wish:

    [( )] ...
    [(X)] <-- Only the **X** is correct.
    [( )] ...

### Gap Text

The capital of France is [[ Paris ]] and of Italy [[ (Rome) | Milan | Naples ]].

## Survey

How do you like LiaScript so far?

    [(1)] great
    [(2)] okay
    [(3)] not yet

## Executable Code

Code blocks with a script tag can be edited and executed:

```javascript
let sum = 0;
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { sum += i; }
sum;
```
<script>@input</script>


### Projects

You can make your code executable and define projects:

``` js     -EvalScript.js
let who = data.first_name + " " + data.last_name;

if(data.online) {
  who + " is online"; }
else {
  who + " is NOT online"; }
```
``` json    +Data.json
{
  "first_name" :  "Sammy",
  "last_name"  :  "Shark",
  "online"     :  true
}
```
<script>
  // insert the JSON dataset into the local variable data
  let data = @input(1);

  // eval the script that uses this dataset
  eval(`@input(0)`);
</script>

## More

Find out what else you can do:

https://liascript.github.io/course/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/liaScript/docs/master/README.md

Change the numbering style of an ordered list with an attribute comment directly above it:

  type="a" / "A"   letters
  type="i" / "I"   roman numerals

Any CSS list style works as well, e.g. <!-- style="list-style-type: lower-greek" -->.

documentation:
persistent can be used in two places:

In a section header, persistent: true keeps the section alive when the user navigates to another slide. Scripts, widgets and animations are not re-created when the user comes back. This is also needed if scripts on other slides should be able to send events to this section.

In the main header, persistent: false prevents that anything of this course (states and the entry in the local course index) is stored in the browser.

Example:
  ## Live Clock
  <!--
  persistent: true
  -->

  <script>
  setInterval(() => send.output(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()), 1000)
  "LIA: wait"
  </script>
label: lia-macro-persistent

documentation:
Imports the main header of another course or template: its macros, script and link entries, attributions and @onload code, but not its content. Templates of the LiaTemplates collection add features such as music notation, programming languages or 3D models. Use one import line per URL.

Pin a tag or commit in the URL instead of master/main, so that your course does not break when the template changes.

Example:
  <!--
  import: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/liaTemplates/ABCjs/main/README.md
  -->

  ``` abc  @ABCJS.render
  X: 1
  T: Test Tune
  M: C
  L: 1/8
  K: F
  "F"[A3F3][AF] ([AF][GE][AF])[BG] |
  ```

See https://github.com/topics/liascript-template for more templates.
label: lia-macro-import

documentation:
Attribution is an important issue. With the attribute command, you can define the attribution that is showed within the info field within the navigation pannel. These elements get also imported if you import the functionality from another course.

A good attribution might look like the follwing ones...

Example:
  <!--
  attribute: [AlaSQL](https://alasql.org)
             by [Andrey Gershun](agershun@gmail.com)
             & [Mathias Rangel Wulff](m@rawu.dk)
             is licensed under [MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)

  attribute: [PapaParse](https://www.papaparse.com)
             by [Matthew Holt](https://twitter.com/mholt6)
             is licensed under [MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
  -->
label: lia-macro-attribute

documentation:
You can change the default appearance of your document, either if you prefer dark mode or light mode. This will not change the user preferences. The default mode is defined by the user settings.

Example:
  <!--
  dark: true

  dark: false
  -->
label: lia-macro-dark

documentation:
You can change the default style of your document, either if you do not have any effects you can set mode to Textbook or start with and interactive Presentation. The three modes a the same as defined within the document at the upper right button. The default mode is defined by the user settings.

Example:
  <!--
  mode: Presentation

  mode: Slides

  mode: Textbook
  -->
label: lia-macro-mode

documentation:
Disable or enable the classroom feature for your course, by using this macro within the header of your course. You can use words like `false`, `disabled`, `0`, `OFF` ... LiaScript will recognize them as negative. All other words like wouldLoveToSeeThisFeature are treated as positive. __But better stick with `false`/`true`, `on`/`off`, `disable`/`enable`__

Example:
  <!--
  classroom: false
  -->
label: lia-macro-classroom

documentation:
Disable or enable the experimental google translation for your course, by using this macro within the header of your course. You can use words like `false`, `disabled`, `0`, `OFF` ... LiaScript will recognize them as negative. All other words like wouldLoveToSeeThisFeature are treated as positive. __But better stick with `false`/`true`, `on`/`off`, `disable`/`enable`__

Example:

documentation:
Disable or enable sharing for your course, by using this macro within the header (no share-icon and button will be displayed). You can use words like `false`, `disabled`, `0`, `OFF` ... LiaScript will recognize them as negative. All other words like wouldLoveToSeeThisFeature are treated as positive. __But better stick with `false`/`true`, `on`/`off`, `disable`/`enable`__

Example:

documentation:
Use this macro to redefine the respository information of your project, by default the course will display the GitHub, GitLab, or Dropbox origin. By adding this information to the head, you can define a static root for your project, which will also be visible on all exports.

Example:

documentation: If you have a more complex multi-line macro definition, you can also use the following style so that it gets rendered at least in a readable manner by Github for example. Thus, you can place your macro call into into the code-block header, the first (optional) language parameter gets ignored and, whereby the following elements within the block are passed as the last multi-line parameter to that call. Example: ## Macro ```json @panorama("0",https://pannellum.org/images/cerro-toco-0.jpg) { "pitch": 14.1, "yaw": 1.5, "type": "info", "text": "Baltimore Museum of Art", "URL": "https://artbma.org/" }, { "pitch": -0.9, "yaw": 144.4, "type": "info", "text": "North Charles Street" } ```

Example:

  script:   https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/algebrite@1.4.0/dist/algebrite.bundle-for-browser.js
  -->

  ```

documentation:
Header field: links a translated version of the course, which is offered in the translation menu. Repeat it for every language: name of the language followed by the (relative) path or URL.

documentation:

All supported languages: https://github.com/liaScript/lia-localization

documentation:
Header field: the default text-to-speech voice for narration comments (--{{n}}--) and playback buttons. Can be overwritten per section and per comment. Type "voice" to search all voices.

  -->

documentation:
Header block: JavaScript that is executed once when the course is loaded, e.g. to configure a library or to define global helper functions. It is also imported by other courses that import this one.

Example:
  <!--
  script: https://cdn.example.com/library.js

documentation: Calls a macro with parameters. Inside the definition, @0, @1, ... are replaced by the parameters in order. The last parameter can also be passed as a code block directly above the call (see lia-macro-call-block). Commas inside a parameter can be protected with backticks, but this is not reliable in every LiaScript version. If possible, avoid commas in parameters. Example: @highlight(red, simple text)
label: lia-macro-call-params

documentation:
Debugging: an additional @ in front of a macro call shows the expanded result as code instead of executing it. Useful to find out what a macro (or an imported template) really produces.

Example:

label: lia-macro-debug

documentation:
An apostrophe after the @ escapes the result of a macro, so that it can be used safely inside a JavaScript string or template literal (quotes, backticks and backslashes are escaped). Works with @'input, @'input(1), @'0 or @'MacroName(...). Use it only once, otherwise characters are escaped twice.

Example:

  ```

    let text = `@'input`
    text.length
  </script>

documentation:

documentation:
As in common Markdown, a document is segregated into different parts by its titles. A title starts with hash-tag (#) that is followed by an head-line. The number of subsequent hash-tags defines the order. It is furthermore possible to overwrite some of the definitions from the main header, see more information on this by typing "liaheadersection" ...

Example:

  author:  New Author

It is possible to add styling elements to the titles, but this should be used only in some rare cases.

As in common Markdown, a document is segregated into different parts by its titles. A title starts with hash-tag (#) that is followed by an head-line. The number of subsequent hash-tags defines the order. It is furthermore possible to overwrite some of the definitions from the main header, see more information on this by typing "liaheadersection" ...

Example:
  # Main Title

  ...

  ## Chapter Title
  <!--
  comment: This comment is only for demonstrating purposes
           and will be overwritten within the next slide...

  author:  New Author
  email:   notmain@email.com
  -->

  ...

  ### Section __Title__

  ...

It is possible to add styling elements to the titles, but this should be used only in some rare cases.
label: lia-title-4

documentation:
The details and summary tags are standard HTML tags and GitHub also supports their usage with Markdown. These tags offer a neat way to define something what is nowadays called accordion. Thus, your user can click on the summary text to make the body of the details-tag appear.

Example:
  <details>

  <summary>**Honest Textbook ads (click to enlarge)**</summary>

  !?[If High School and College Textbooks Were Honest - Honest Ads](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lhSjYT7pWkw)

  </details>
label: lia-details

documentation:
GitHub-style alert box: a blockquote that starts with [!NOTE]. Useful information that users should know, even when skimming the content. An optional title or emoji can follow the keyword on the same line (GitLab style). The alert renders as a normal quote in other Markdown viewers.

Available types: NOTE, TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION

Example:
  > [!NOTE]
  > Useful information that users should know, even when skimming the content.

  > [!NOTE] ℹ️ Custom title
  > The title replaces the default one.
insertText:
> [!NOTE]
> Useful information that users should know, even when skimming the content.
label: lia-alert-note

documentation:
GitHub-style alert box: a blockquote that starts with [!TIP]. Helpful advice for doing things better or more easily. An optional title or emoji can follow the keyword on the same line (GitLab style). The alert renders as a normal quote in other Markdown viewers.

Available types: NOTE, TIP, IMPORTANT, WARNING, CAUTION

Example:

documentation:
Every heading (#, ##, ###, ...) starts a new slide. To use headings inside a slide without creating new slides, wrap them in a <section> or <article> tag. Leave blank lines around the content, so that it is parsed as Markdown.

Example:
  # Slide Title

  <section>

  ## Part A

  Some text.

  </section>
insertText:
<section>

## Grouped Sub-Heading

Content that stays on this slide.

</section>
label: lia-section

documentation:
Setext-style headings (text underlined with === or ---) do not start a new slide and do not appear in the table of contents. Use them for local structure within a slide.

  ===   -> large local heading
  ---   -> smaller local heading

Example:
  ## Section Title

  Local Subsection
  ================

  Local Sub-Subsection
  --------------------
label: lia-title-setext

documentation:
Everything inside is passed through as raw HTML: no Markdown parsing and no indentation checks. Useful for complex hand-written HTML, such as tables with rowspan or colspan. Example:
AB
C
label: lia-keep

documentation:
A comment that starts with three or more dashes (<!--- ... --->) is dropped completely by LiaScript. A normal HTML comment (<!-- ... -->) is read as attributes for the next element. Use it for notes to yourself or to comment out content.

Important: always leave a blank line between this comment and any other HTML comment (e.g. a styling or chart comment). Two comments without a blank line are merged by the Markdown parser and the following element is shown as plain text.

Example:
  <!---
  TODO: add a better picture here
  --->

  <!-- data-type="LinePlot" -->
  | x | y |
  |---|---|
  | 1 | 2 |
insertText:
<!---
This note is ignored by LiaScript.
--->
label: lia-comment-ignore

documentation:
Style any block (paragraph, list, table, quote, code, ...) by placing an HTML comment with attributes directly above it. Any HTML attribute works, e.g. style, class or id. The comment is invisible in other Markdown viewers.

Example:
  <!-- style="color: purple; font-size: 1.2em" class="animated rollIn" -->
  This whole paragraph is styled.

  <!-- style="width: 50%" -->
  | <!-- style="background: azure" --> Header 1 | Header 2 |
  |:--------------------------------------------|:---------|
  | <!-- style="background: coral" --> Item 1   | Item 2   |
insertText:
<!-- style="color: purple; font-size: 1.2em;" class="animated rollIn" -->
This whole paragraph is styled.
label: lia-style-block

documentation:
Style an inline element (bold text, a link, an image, a formula, ...) by placing an HTML comment with attributes directly after it, without a space.

Example:
  This **is important**<!-- style="color: red" --> text.

  ![a lion](lion.svg)<!-- style="width: 300px;" class="animated bounce" -->
label: lia-style-inline

documentation:
A <script> tag in the text (without a code block) is a JavaScript component. It runs automatically when the slide is shown, and the value of its last expression is displayed in place, like an inline element. If the result is undefined, nothing is shown.

Every script has its own scope. To share values between scripts, attach them to window. Scripts can be combined with animations ({1}{<script>...</script>}) to run them at a certain step.

Example:
  $ \sin(\frac{\pi}{2}) = $ <script>Math.sin(Math.PI / 2)</script>

  Today is <script>new Date().toLocaleDateString()</script>.
label: lia-script-inline

documentation:
Turns a script into a small interactive widget. input="..." selects an HTML5 input type, value="..." sets the initial value, and @input is replaced by the current value before the script runs. The result is shown next to the input.

text, number, range, radio, select and checkbox run on every change. button runs on load and on every click. submit only runs when clicked. The other types (date, time, color, ...) run when the field loses focus.

Extra attributes: min, max, step, options="a|b|c" (radio/select), default="..." (text shown before the first run of button/submit).

Example:
  <script input="number" value="1" min="0" max="100">
  let i = @input
  "Square of " + i + " = " + i * i
  </script>
insertText:
<script input="text" value="Hello World">
let str = "@input"
str.split("").reverse().join("")
</script>
label: lia-script-input

documentation:
A slider that re-runs the script on every change. @input is replaced by the current number.

Example:
  <script input="range" value="0" min="0" max="360" step="1">
  let deg = @input
  "sin(" + deg + "°) = " + Math.sin(deg * Math.PI / 180).toFixed(3)
  </script>
insertText:
<script input="range" value="0" min="0" max="360" step="1">
let deg = @input
"sin(" + deg + "°) = " + Math.sin(deg * Math.PI / 180).toFixed(3)
</script>
label: lia-script-input-range

documentation:
A dropdown (select) or a group of radio buttons. The options are separated by | in the options attribute, value sets the initial selection.

Example:
  <script input="radio" value="1" options="1|2|3|Hello World">
  "Selected option: @input"
  </script>
label: lia-script-input-select

documentation:
A button that runs the script only when it is clicked. default sets the text that is shown before the first click. Use input="button" instead to run it also once on load.

Example:
  <script input="submit" default="roll the dice">
  Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1
  </script>
label: lia-script-input-submit

documentation:
Connect scripts: a script with output="name" publishes its current result. Other scripts on the same slide can read it with @input(`name`) (with backticks) and re-run automatically when it changes.

If two scripts depend on each other, give both a default="..." value. Otherwise the first calculation fails.

Example:
  <script input="checkbox" value="true" output="P" default="true">
  @input
  </script>
  AND
  <script input="checkbox" value="false" output="Q" default="false">
  @input
  </script>
  =
  <script>
  @input(`P`) && @input(`Q`)
  </script>
label: lia-script-connect

documentation:
Formats the result of a script with the JavaScript Intl API for the given locale. Only the display changes, connected scripts still get the raw value.

  format="number"        1234.5 -> 1.234,5 (de-DE)
  format="datetime"      dates and times
  format="relativetime"  "in 3 days"
  format="list"          "a, b and c"
  format="pluralrules"   plural category

Example:
  <script input="date" value="2024-05-16" format="datetime" locale="de">
  "@input"
  </script>
label: lia-script-format

documentation:
A self-updating script component: return "LIA: wait" (or call send.wait()) to keep it running, then call send.output(...) for every update. The process keeps running in the background when the user switches slides, until send.stop() is called.

send.output only works in standalone scripts, not in scripts of code blocks (use send.lia there).

Shortcuts: send.wait(), send.stop(), send.clear()

Example:
  <script>
  setInterval(() => send.output(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()), 1000)
  "LIA: wait"
  </script>
insertText:
<script>
let i = 0
setInterval(function() {
  i++
  send.output("counting " + i)
}, 1000)
"LIA: wait"
</script>
label: lia-script-counter

documentation:
Every script runs in its own local scope, so variables of one script are not visible in another. To share values between scripts, attach them to window explicitly. For live updates between scripts, prefer output="..." and @input(`...`) (see lia-script-connect).

Example:
  <script> window.a = 22 ** 3 </script>
  <script> window.a / 2 </script>
label: lia-script-window

documentation:
LIA.classroom lets scripts exchange messages with all participants of a live classroom session (peer-to-peer). It is only active while a classroom is connected.

  LIA.classroom.connected                 true if a session is active
  LIA.classroom.on("connect", cb)         also "disconnect"
  LIA.classroom.publish("topic", data)    send to all peers
  LIA.classroom.subscribe("topic", cb)    returns an id
  LIA.classroom.unsubscribe(id)

Example:
  <script>
  LIA.classroom.on("connect", () => send.output("connected"))
  "LIA: wait"
  </script>
insertText:
<script>
if (LIA.classroom.connected) {
  const id = LIA.classroom.subscribe("topic", (message) => {
    send.output(JSON.stringify(message))
  })
  LIA.classroom.publish("topic", { hello: "world" })
}
"LIA: wait"
</script>
label: lia-script-classroom

documentation:
Surveys use the quiz brackets but have no correct answer, only a submit button. Three or more underscores in double brackets create a one-line text input.

In a live classroom session, the answers of one-line inputs are shown as a word cloud, where comma-separated terms are counted. Use it for keywords or short phrases.

Example:
  Which programming languages do you know? Separate them with commas.

      [[___]]
label: lia-survey-text-line

documentation:
A multi-line text survey (textarea). Every group of underscores separated by a space adds one row. The number of groups sets the number of rows, the length of a group does not matter. One pair of double brackets always creates exactly one input field. For several fields, write several surveys, each with its own question above it.

In a live classroom session, the answers of a textarea are listed one below the other, which suits longer answers.

Example:
  A two-line text survey:

      [[___ ___]]

  Please describe your opinion in a few sentences:

      [[___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___]]
label: lia-survey-text

documentation:
Single-choice survey: like a single-choice quiz, but the parentheses contain an identifier instead of an X. Numeric identifiers let the classroom view plot the results as a distribution, while text identifiers are shown as categories. Identifiers do not have to be ordered or sequential.

Example:

  Choose between different options:

    [(1)] option 1
    [(2)] option 2
    [(0)] option 3

  What is your favorite color:

    [(red)]   red?
    [(blue)]  blue?
    [(green)] green?
label: lia-survey-single-choice

documentation:
Multiple-choice survey: like a multiple-choice quiz, but the brackets contain an identifier instead of an X. Start an identifier with a number (e.g. [[1 red]]) to get a numeric instead of a categorical representation in the classroom view.

Example:

  Choose as many options as your want:

    [[1]] option 1
    [[2]] option 2
    [[0]] option 0

  Mark all colors you like:

    [[red]]   red?
    [[blue]]  blue?
    [[green]] green?
    [[none]]  None of these ...
label: lia-survey-multiple-choice

documentation:
Single-choice matrix survey: the header contains the column identifiers in parentheses, every following row ([ ] + text) becomes its own single-choice question. Identifiers can be numbers or words.

Example:

  Give marks:

      [(-1)(0)(1)]
      [          ] LiaScript is great?
      [          ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [          ] I would use it for online **surveys**?

  What is your opinion:

      [(agree)(unsure)(maybe not so)]
      [                             ] LiaScript is great?
      [                             ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [                             ] I would use it for online **surveys**?
label: lia-survey-single-choice-matrix

documentation:
Multiple-choice matrix survey: the header contains the column identifiers in brackets, every following row ([ ] + text) becomes its own multiple-choice question. Identifiers can be numbers or words.

Example:

  Give marks:

      [[-1][0][1]]
      [          ] LiaScript is great?
      [          ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [          ] I would use it for online **surveys**?

  What is your opinion:

      [[agree][unsure][maybe not so]]
      [                             ] LiaScript is great?
      [                             ] I would use it to make online **courses**?
      [                             ] I would use it for online **surveys**?
label: lia-survey-multiple-choice-matrix

documentation:
A script directly after a survey can check or process the input before it is accepted. Empty input is rejected by default. The last expression decides:

  true                              -> accept the input
  false                             -> reject it silently
  send.lia("message", [], false)    -> reject it with a message

Wrap @input in backticks for text surveys. For choice surveys @input is the selected value(s). console.log does not show anything here, use alert(...) while developing.

Example:
      [[___]]
      <script>
        let input = `@input`.trim();
        if (input.length > 4) true
        else send.lia("Please provide some meaningful input", [], false)
      </script>
label: lia-survey-js

documentation:
SVG can be written directly into the document. It must not be put into a code block, otherwise it is shown as code. Use viewBox to make the image scale with the slide width.

Dark mode inverts the colors of LiaScript but not the hard-coded colors of an SVG, so set a background and explicit colors on the svg element.

Example:
  <svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" style="background: white;">
    <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="lightblue" stroke="blue"/>
    <text x="50" y="55" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">Circle</text>
  </svg>
insertText:
<svg viewBox="0 0 200 100" style="background: white;">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="lightblue" stroke="blue" stroke-width="2"/>
  <rect x="110" y="10" width="80" height="80" fill="lightgreen" stroke="green" stroke-width="2"/>
</svg>
label: lia-svg

documentation:
foreignObject places LiaScript content (Markdown, formulas, quizzes, animations, ...) at a position inside an SVG. x, y, width and height are required and use the coordinates of the viewBox.

Example:
  <svg viewBox="0 0 280 200" style="background: white;">
  <foreignObject x="130" y="0" width="200" height="80">
  Circumference:

  $$C = 2 \pi r$$
  </foreignObject>
  <circle cx="100" cy="100" r="80" fill="lightblue" stroke="blue"/>
  <line x1="100" y1="100" x2="180" y2="100" stroke="red"/>
  <foreignObject x="110" y="78" width="100" height="30"> Radius: $r$ </foreignObject>
  </svg>
insertText:
<svg viewBox="0 0 280 200" style="background: white;">
<circle cx="100" cy="100" r="80" fill="lightblue" stroke="blue" stroke-width="2"/>
<line x1="100" y1="100" x2="180" y2="100" stroke="red" stroke-width="2"/>
<foreignObject x="110" y="70" width="100" height="30">
Radius: $r$
</foreignObject>
</svg>
label: lia-svg-foreignobject

documentation:
There must be at least 3 dashes separating each header cell. Cells are separated by pipes (|), and you don't need to make the raw Markdown line up prettily. Hyphens (-) are used to separate the table header from the body, whereby the colons are used to align the columns.

Example:

| Tables        | Are           | Cool  |
| ------------- |:-------------:| -----:|
| col 3 is      | right-aligned | $1600 |
| col 2 is      | centered      |   $12 |
| zebra stripes | are neat      |    $1 |
